title: Engine: rear main seal & bottom-end refresh
goal: Replace the leaking rear main seal and refresh the bottom end (new main and rod bearings, water pump, timing cover) without a full rebuild, then put the engine back in the car.
summary: The 1968 302 (from a Fairlane) leaked at the rear main. A previous owner had siliconed the upper seal half into the block, so the crank has to come out. A chip also broke off the rear of the block while the old seal was being punched out. The engine is already out of the car (the C4 stays in) and torn down on a stand, waiting on parts. Heads, pistons, rods and cam stay in; cam timing returns exactly by going back together dot to dot. Since the crank is out anyway, the job grew to include new bearings, a water pump and a timing cover. On Oct 30 the crank was turned a couple of times with the chain off; a compression or leak-down test after reassembly will confirm no valves were bent. Merged from two chats: an earlier one (engine pull, chipped block) and a later one (bottom end).
next_step: When the micrometer arrives, measure the journals, then order bearings, a water pump and a new timing cover (the old one is cracked). Meanwhile: sand the JB Weld repair and clean the old seal and silicone out of the grooves.

subprojects.title: Pull the engine (C4 stays in the car)
subprojects.goal: Engine out of the car and on the stand, with the transmission left in the car.
subprojects.summary: Engine separated at the bellhousing and lifted out the top. The C4 automatic and its torque converter stay in the car, with the transmission supported by a jack or stand and the converter strapped so it can't slide off the front pump.
notes: The pull itself is done (engine is on the stand). One safety check is left open on purpose: confirm the converter is strapped and the transmission is supported.

On reinstall, verify the converter is fully seated on the pump (it drops over it with 2-3 distinct engagements) before mating the engine, and don't draw it forward with the converter bolts. The converter-to-flexplate fastener count is typically 4 on a C4; verify on the car.

subprojects.goal: Crank out with rods, main caps and shells laid out in order; heads, pistons, rods and cam stay in.

notes: 2026-10-30 INCIDENT: the crank was turned a couple of times after the chain was off. It turned smoothly with no hard stop, so valve contact is very unlikely. A compression or leak-down test after reassembly will confirm it (see Startup and verification). Don't turn the crank again until it's out. When it goes back in, set the keyway to match the dot-to-dot photo before the chain goes on.
The guide measures crank endplay before teardown. If that wasn't done, measure it after reassembly only.
Safest order is rods off with the chain still on, then the timing set. With the chain off, don't turn the crank or cam more than a few degrees.
Upside down on the stand, the crank lifts straight up out of the uncapped rods; rods don't need pushing (guide corrected Oct 30).

subprojects.title: Assess the chipped block
subprojects.goal: Know whether the chip at the rear of the block affects the seal groove, and fix it if it does.
subprojects.summary: While punching out the old seal, a chip broke off the very rear of the block (transmission side). Believed non-structural; it only matters if it breaks into the groove where the seal's outer diameter seats.
notes: From the earlier chat, which was written before the crank was out. With the crank out, the whole upper groove is now visible, so no mirror-and-feel guesswork is needed.

If it's the rear edge or chamfer only, it is not a sealing surface: proceed as normal. If part of the groove wall is gone: a dab of anaerobic sealant or RTV on the seal OD at that spot, or fill the void with epoxy (low-stress, non-bearing area).
Whether the chip has already been looked at is not recorded in the newer chat.

subprojects.title: Rear main seal
subprojects.goal: Old seal and all silicone out; new two-piece seal installed correctly and not leaking.
subprojects.summary: A previous owner siliconed the upper seal half into the block. The lower half came out of the cap; the upper half wouldn't move, which is why the crank comes out.
notes: Correct technique: sealant on the seal ends only, lube the lip, and offset the seal parting lines from the cap-to-block split. Leftover RTV in the bore is the number one cause of a repeat leak.
The seal is not in the Summit cart yet (as of Nov 2); see Parts and tools ordering.

tasks.text: Drive out the small pin in the cap's seal groove, if there is one
tasks.detail: Left over from the rope seal; it stops a rubber seal from seating.

tasks.text: Clean old sealant off the rear cap's mating faces and the matching block faces
Check the crank's seal surface
tasks.detail: Fingernail test: if a groove catches your nail, ask a crank shop. A grooved or scored journal where the lip rides makes the new seal leak too; if it's worn, plan a thin repair sleeve (e.g. Speedi-Sleeve) before reassembly rather than hoping a new seal fixes it. Condition is unknown until inspected.

subprojects.title: Crank inspection and journal cleanup
subprojects.goal: Journals cleaned and measured so the right bearing size can be chosen.
subprojects.summary: A couple of small nicks on the journals. Knock down burrs, clean, then measure with the micrometer to choose bearing size. Measuring waits on the micrometer.
notes: Remove the raised burr, not the dent. Oiled 400/600 grit emery or wet/dry in a shoeshine motion, then crocus cloth. No Scotch-Brite. Stay off the fillets.
Mains about 2.249 in., rods about 2.123 in.; taper and out-of-round under about 0.0005 in. is healthy. Over that, show the crank to a machine shop.
The crank seal-surface check (and Speedi-Sleeve option) is under Rear main seal.

decisions.text: Scope: the crank comes out; nothing else does. Heads, pistons, rods and cam stay in. The timing chain only has to come off the crank sprocket. (Date approximate: start of the chat.)

No re-degreeing: cam timing is set by the sprocket keyways and dots, so going back dot to dot on the same keyway restores it exactly. Re-degree only if the cam, sprockets or an adjustable setting change. (Date approximate.)
Order matters for the valves: rods off with the chain still on, then the timing set. With the chain off, don't turn the crank or cam more than a few degrees. (Date approximate.)
Rods don't need pushing: upside down on the stand the crank lifts straight out of the uncapped rods. The guide step about pushing rods was wrong and was corrected.
Clockwise rotation (from the front) is the habit, not a hard rule: it keeps chain slack on the correct side so the dots read true. A little backward by accident does no harm. (Date approximate.)
Turning the engine dry by hand on the stand is fine. Avoid spinning it fast or for many turns, keep grit off the bearings, oil bare journals and bores if it sits. (Date approximate.)
Replace the water pump now; it must match inlet side, length, rotation and fittings. (Date approximate.)
Timing cover: originally planned to reuse after inspecting for coolant-passage corrosion; now replacing. (Date approximate.)

Journal nicks: remove the raised burr, not the dent. Oiled 400/600 grit then crocus; no Scotch-Brite. Summit's emery is only 120/180 grit; use Goodson UR-1-CROCUS or hardware-store sheets. (Date approximate.)
Feeler gauges instead of a $50 dial indicator for crank endplay. (Date approximate.)
Cam isn't new, so this isn't a new-cam break-in, but use high-zinc oil or a ZDDP additive for the flat-tappet cam on every oil change. (Date approximate.)

Obsolete, kept for the record: engine hoist plan was to buy a Harbor Freight 2-ton foldable (~$270) or borrow an AutoZone Loan-A-Tool loaner, not a daily/weekly rental (the hoist sits idle through the long middle of the job). The engine is already out. Still needed again at reinstall. (Date approximate; earlier chat.)
Obsolete, kept for the record: no transmission jack needed because the C4 stays in the car; a floor jack or stand with a 2x4 pad is enough. (Date approximate; earlier chat.)
